Press Release:


Brussels Bombings
The world unites in condemning the deadly bomb blasts that this week saw more than 30 people killed and around 230 injured in Belgium. The Islamic State has claimed responsibility for the attacks. John Webb reports from Brussels, a city in mourning.


Script:


John VO:
On the evening of Tuesday the 22nd of March, Belgian security forces encircled an apartment in a Brussels suburb. It was believed to be a safe house for a group of terrorists linked to the Islamic State.

John link:
The taxi driver had earlier that day driven 3 men to Brussels Airport, little knowing that the apartment contained vital clues about their background.

John VO:
Investigators found footage filmed by the men showing they were monitoring a nuclear facility outside Brussels as well as scientist who worked there. It’s speculated that they were trying to find a way in – either to steal nuclear material or blow the facility up.
But they appear to have abandoned that mission and instead on the morning before the raid they carried out their plan B.


John VO:
On Tuesday morning a series of devastating suicide bomb blasts erupted in Brussels killing 31 people and injuring at least 260 others. It has been called the worst violence on Belgian soil since World War 2. It came just months after the deadly Paris attacks, realizing Belgium’s worst fears.

John link:
Well it’s about 10 o’clock in the morning on Thursday – We’re heading into Brussels by rail from Paris because the airports in Belgium are still in a state of lock-down and the only way into the country is by car or by train. There was significant security in place in Paris when we left and we’re expecting it to be doubly so when we get to our destination.

John VO:
As expected, the military was out in full force at Brussels Central Station when we arrived with everyone being searched. The mood was sober and resolute. The city was experiencing major delays on the rail system due to the strict security that had been implemented.

John link:
After the Paris attacks in November last year there was a great deal of speculation about which city would be targeted next and the general consensus even back then in Europe at least it would be Brussels.

John VO:
Leading up to the bombings was the capture of Europe’s most wanted fugitive, Salah Abdeslam, who had been in hiding since November. He was shot and wounded by authorities in an anti-terror raid in the Brussels suburb of Molenbeek. Four other people were also arrested.

John VO:
Within hours of Abdeslam’s arrest, Belgium police were assaulted by residents of Molenbeek, who were defending their depraved hero. Riot police with dogs had to be called to the scene.
Then on Tuesday, perhaps in retaliation of the arrests, three suspects entered the departures terminal of Brussels Airport at 7:55am.

Surveillance footage shows them pushing trolleys with bombs disguised as luggage.

Three minutes later gunfire was reportedly heard followed by an explosion. As passengers started running, a second blast exploded 10 seconds later. One of the attackers was identified as Ibrahim El Bakraoui. The second attacker is known IS bomb-maker Najim Laachraoui. Both died in the explosion. A third suspect, wearing a light-colored jacket and a hat, fled the airport. He was later caught on Friday during raids and has been identied as “Faycal C”. He left a large bag. Just before the bomb squad arrived, this bag exploded due to the instability of the explosives.

John Link:
About an hour and 15 minutes after the airport explosions, another device was detonated, this time at the city’s busy Maelbeek metro station.
John VO:
The explosion occurred in the second train car, which was still in the station.
The attacker was identified by his fingerprints as Khalid el Bakraoui, brother of one of the airport bombers.
John VO:
FRANÇOIS JANNE D’OTHÉE is a freelance journalist working in Brussels
John: You had some interesting views on why they chose the Maelbeek Metro Station why do you think they did that?
Francois:
I think that they choose that Maelbeek Metro station because its in the centre of the European district. if you in the inside of the metro station the building is compact and if you put a bomb inside there could be very high consequences.
John: Given that it was inevitable that Belgians were expecting it do you think that more could have been done to try and prevent it or is this something that is impossible for police?

Francois: How can you prevent attacks in the Metro? It’s impossible.
John VO:
The South African Embassy in Brussels is a mere 800m from station. Ambassador Mxolisi Nkosi took the unusual step to close the embassy for safety reasons.
John VO:
He says while Brussels was the target, the bombers message was aimed at a bigger audience.
Ambassador Nkosi:
I think the message is targeted at the Belgium government and also at the EU and its institutions in the main. But generally it’s a message targeted at the world.
Strike Link
Ambassador Nkosi: We have to fight this - we have to collectively wage a war against terror.
John VO:
That sense of unity was on display at Palais de la Bourse- it is where Brussels residents have gathered to remember those who lost their lives in the attacks. It’s an unusual display in a country which has a long history of division.
Link at square
John VO:
Regis Dandoy is a professor of political science at the university of Couvain and he says Belgium remains a divided country because of it’s history of tension between the various language groups. That problem is amplified in Brussels with a significant immigrant population.
Regis:
John VO:
It’s in this environment that Belgium has become fertile ground for isolation and extremism.
John VO:
Originally from Umhlanga, Kirsty Reid has lived in Belgium for 12 years. She works at the European Commission and was at the office when she heard about the airport bombings.
Kirsty: The metro line, Brussels is a very small city and we only have a very small metro system, so it’s a metro line that everyone uses to get to the office, and one that we use daily... so it’s definitely something that you... there are moments in your life where you’ll always remember where you were, and this is definitely one of them.

John VO:
That a plan was being hatched to bring terror to the streets ofg Brussels came as a great shock to South African couple Barry and Coreen de Vaal. They run a guesthouse owned by the local Christian ministry less than a kilometer away from the bombers refuge.
Coreen de Vaal
John VO:
Belgian security forces meanwhile continue to conduct raids across Brussels as the net closes on other terror suspects. For Kirsty the safety of her child in this uncertain environment is her main priority.

Kirsty bite

John VO:
Part of that impact is likely to see Belgium confront it’s differences in an effort to put up a united front.

John VO:
South African Masters student Sheena Ramkumar is studying philosophy in the town of Leuven 30 kilometers from Brussels.


John You seem to suggest in some ways there maybe something positive to extract from this there maybe a way of forging a new Belgium identity…?

Regis 09:29- Well this is the Belgian ??? When we suffered a lot during the last century two world wars a lot of problems endemic political problems these community and linguistic fights between the Flemish and French speakers, so Belgians have suffered a lot but have learnt how to grow out of these challenges or these difficulties and probably Belgium tomorrow will be different from what we seen yesterday and I think we should not underestimate this capacity of Belgians it is resilience of the Belgian people this capacity of react adapt to these changing and terror circumstances.

John VO:
If they are to adapt Belgians are starting to realize that events in Syria and Iraq – where the Islamic State are strongest – will have an impact on their own The scale of the challenge was again demonstrated this week when a suspected IS suicide bomber blew himself up at a soccer stadium in Iraq. 32 people were killed.

John VO:
The effects of the civil war in Syria are also reverberating through Europe, particularly in Belgium where an alarming number of it’s young Muslim citizens are joining the the IS cause.

John: In a lot of ways it does feel that the conflicts are growing closer together. Syria doesn’t seem that far anymore. Do you know what I mean? It’s as the conflict is being brought to people’s door steps.

Francois: Syria was a completely unknown country to the Belgium people, I mean we have no close relations with Syria.

it was not till end of December 2012 suddenly we realized that there is something abnormal by these young people living in Belgium to fight in Syria.

John VO:
But while their government is left to confront that reality, ordinary Belgians say now is a time to grieve.



Promos:

After months of tension, Belgium’s worst fears have been realized when series of devastating bomb blasts shook Brussels. We travel to a city on lock down.

Sound up

More IS attacks in Brussels with investigators uncovering a plot more terrifying than they could have imagined. Did Tuesday’s attackers have a much more sinister target in mind?

Sound up
